summary: Flame in Freefall is an interactive web dashboard that shows whether NASA has the fire safety data needed for the habitats we are about to build. NASA has proposed 34% oxygen at about 8 psi for the lunar base, an atmosphere where materials ignite far more easily than in normal air. We mapped 19 microgravity combustion investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository by oxygen, pressure and airflow, and compared them with Artemis habitats and past fires such as Apollo 1. Users pick a habitat, and the app ranks the most relevant experiments, reveals data gaps and offers an AI copilot that answers questions citing experiments by ID. We also built a physics-based model, trained on ISS data, that predicts whether a cabin material keeps burning. It correctly classified 13 of 16 centrifuge tests it never saw. We found that PSI has no published data for solids or smoke in Artemis conditions, and that cutting ventilation stops a fire on the ISS but not on the Moon. This matters because in a spacecraft there is nowhere to run. Our tool helps NASA prioritize the next experiments and helps designers choose safer materials and sensors.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard for people designing habitats on the Moon and Mars. Artemis habitats are expected to use about 34 % oxygen at 8.2 psi, against 21 % at 14.7 psi on Earth and on the ISS. More oxygen makes materials ignite more easily, and in microgravity flames behave very differently: no buoyancy, a spherical flame fed by slow diffusion. Our question was simple: do we actually know how fire behaves in the air crews will breathe there?

The dashboard walks the user through six steps:

1. Pick a habitat (ISS, lunar rover, lunar base, Mars habitat, spacesuit) or a past incident (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir, Artemis II). Each one sets oxygen, pressure, ventilation and gravity.

2. See an animated flame that changes with those conditions: a sphere in microgravity, stretched upward as gravity increases. Three plain sentences explain why.

3. Get a prediction from our own model: the probability that a burning cabin material (PMMA, acrylic) keeps burning, the minimum oxygen it needs, the habitat's margin above that limit, and what happens if the fans are turned off. Every number comes with a 95 % interval.

4. See whether NASA has data for that atmosphere, for four fire types: materials, liquids, gases and smoke. A coverage map places all investigations by oxygen and pressure next to the habitats.

5. Browse a ranking of 19 NASA combustion investigations by closeness of test conditions and relevance to prevention, detection or suppression, each with its official PSI record (objective, hypothesis, DOI, publications).

6. Ask a copilot free questions. It answers from the closest investigations and our model, and cites them by name.

The prediction model was built by the team. We fit a physics-based flammability boundary, limiting O2 = A + B/u + C·u (radiative extinction at low airflow, blowoff at high airflow), to NASA's BASS-II results from the ISS, and added a term for the airflow that gravity itself creates. We calibrated that term with leave-one-gravity-level-out cross-validation and validated the model on 16 partial-gravity centrifuge tests from a separate study that the model never saw. It predicts the limit within 0.16 points of O2 and classifies 13 of 16 tests correctly.

KEY FINDINGS

- In NASA's public PSI repository, every test with real solid materials ran at 21 % oxygen or less. The planned lunar base uses 34 %. NASA has run closer tests (Saffire-V, Saffire-VI, SoFIE), but that data is not in PSI yet.

- In microgravity the most dangerous airflow for PMMA is about 3.3 cm/s. On the Moon, gravity alone moves the air at about 3.2 cm/s, so a lunar habitat sits at the worst point of the curve.

- Turning off ventilation drops the chance that a PMMA fire keeps burning to 36 % on the ISS, but it stays at 100 % on the Moon.

- To make PMMA non-flammable on the Moon, oxygen would need to drop below 13.8 %, which at 8.2 psi is less than half of what people breathe. Safety has to come from material choice, early detection and suppression.

BENEFITS

Engineers, researchers and students can see in one place what NASA has measured, how close it is to a planned habitat, and where the gaps are. Scattered PSI records become ranked, cited answers. Non-experts can follow the guided steps; experts can open the full map, the PSI records and the notebook.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want the dashboard to help decide which experiments to run next (high oxygen, low pressure, partial gravity, such as LUCI and FM2) and which materials and sensors need testing for Artemis habitats. As new data reaches PSI, it can be added to the same atlas and model, so the gaps close over time. On Earth, the same question applies to oxygen-rich settings like hospitals, submarines and aircraft.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It flips the usual question. Instead of only summarizing what NASA measured, it shows what has not been measured for the places we are going.

- The visuals are generated by code, not images: a halftone flame that reacts to oxygen, gravity and airflow, and halftone planets for each habitat.

- It combines physics and machine learning. We compared our physics model with logistic regression and XGBoost and found that, with little and noisy data, a model with physics inside and four parameters beats a flexible one. XGBoost memorized the noise and could not extrapolate to 34 % oxygen.

- It turns a model result into a practical safety insight: a fire strategy that works on the ISS (cutting ventilation) does not work on the Moon.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Data honesty. Our exploratory analysis showed that NASA runs these tests right at the edge of the limit, so single outcomes are noisy: 11 nearly identical test pairs had opposite results, and even NASA's own curve gets 55 % of single tests right. So we predict the limit, not each test, and we show this in the notebook.

- Validation without leakage. Training data (ISS) and test data (centrifuge, partial gravity) come from different studies, and the gravity term was calibrated without seeing the level being predicted.

- Limits stated clearly. The model covers one material (PMMA) with data near 1 atm. Lower pressure usually burns slightly less, so our predictions lean to the safe side.

- Accessibility. A guided, plain-language flow for non-experts, keyboard support, reduced-motion support, and an offline mode for the copilot if the AI service is down.

- Transparent AI use. The copilot is labeled and only explains our results and NASA records; the prediction itself comes from our own model.

Web app: Next.js 15, React 19 and TypeScript, with hand-made SVG charts and canvas animations, deployed on Vercel.

Model: Python with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, XGBoost, matplotlib and Jupyter.

Copilot: Google Gemini through an OpenAI-compatible API.

Development: an AI coding assistant (Claude) helped write code and extract published data points; the team chose the idea and approach, and reviewed the code and data.

Data: NASA PSI investigation records, the BASS-II summary report and published NASA studies.
